authoredPrompt: This figure stacks five drawings of the same fixed string. At the top a horizontal line runs between two black endpoint dots, each labeled "Node", with a double-headed dimension arrow above it labeled L. Beneath come four standing-wave patterns on lines of that same length, labeled at the left n = 1, n = 2, n = 3, and n = 4. Each is a dark blue curve with a pale mirror-image curve, the two outlining the envelope the string sweeps, ends pinned and interior crossing points rising from none to three. Two expressions sit to the right of each: 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2/1 L, then lambda_2 = L and lambda_2 = 2/2 L, then 3/2 lambda_3 = L and lambda_3 = 2/3 L, then 4/2 lambda_4 = L and lambda_4 = 2/4 L. A general statement closes the lower right, lambda_n = 2/n L for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Holding one length fixed while packing in more half-wavelengths shows how the pinned ends restrict which wavelengths fit. The sequence introduces the normal modes of a string fixed at both ends.
authoredInteractions:
- Button/state for mode number: the learner steps through n = 1, 2, 3, and 4, the standing-wave shape, interior nodes, and wavelength equation update, making clear that exactly n half-wavelengths must fit inside length L.
- Animation for the selected mode: the learner presses play for any mode, the string oscillates between the two envelope curves while endpoint and interior nodes stay fixed, making clear the difference between nodes and antinodes.
- Slider for string length L: the learner drags the endpoint separation, the displayed wavelength for the selected mode stretches or contracts with the string, making clear the relationship lambda_n = 2L/n.
authoredContext:
The lab setup shows a string attached to a string vibrator, which oscillates the string with an adjustable frequency f. The other end of the string passes over a frictionless pulley and is tied to a hanging mass. The magnitude of the tension in the string is equal to the weight of the hanging mass. The string has a constant linear density (mass per length) μ and the speed at which a wave travels down the string equals v=FTμ=mgμ another section. The symmetrical boundary conditions (a node at each end) dictate the possible frequencies that can excite standing waves. Starting from a frequency of zero and slowly increasing the frequency, the first mode n=1 appears as shown in the figure. The first mode, also called the fundamental mode or the first harmonic, shows half of a wavelength has formed, so the wavelength is equal to twice the length between the nodes λ1=2L. The standing wave patterns that are possible for a string, the first four of which are shown in the figure, are known as the normal modes, with frequencies known as the normal frequencies. In summary, the first frequency to produce a normal mode is called the fundamental frequency (or first harmonic). Any frequencies above the fundamental frequency are overtones. The second frequency of the n=2 normal mode of the string is the first overtone (or second harmonic). The frequency of the n=3 normal mode is the second overtone (or third harmonic) and so on.

Standing waves created on a string of length L. A node occurs at each end of the string. The nodes are boundary conditions that limit the possible frequencies that excite standing waves. (Note that the amplitudes of the oscillations have been kept constant for visualization. The standing wave patterns possible on the string are known as the normal modes. Conducting this experiment in the lab would result in a decrease in amplitude as the frequency increases.)

Four figures of a string of length L are shown. Each has two waves. The first one has 1 node. It is labeled half lambda 1 = L, lambda 1 = 2 by 1 times L. The second figure has 2 nodes. It is labeled lambda 2 = L, lambda 2 = 2 by 2 times L. The third figure has three nodes. It is labeled 3 by 2 times lambda 3 = L, lambda 3 = 2 by 3 times L. The fourth figure has 4 nodes. It is labeled 4 by 2 times lambda 4 = L, lambda 4 = 2 by 4 times L. There is a derived formula at the bottom, lambda n equal to 2 by n times L for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.
